title: Investigating Italian disinformation spreading on Twitter in the context of 2019 European elections
screen_reason: Included for CONCENTRATION only. The corpus is an all-disinformation corpus (all tweets carrying links to 63 blacklisted Italian disinformation websites) with NO denominator of overall Italian political tweets, so no prevalence, exposure or sharing share can be computed. But the paper states the sharing concentration explicitly: about 20% of the sharing community (~4k of 23,243 users) accounts for more than 90% of the 354,746 disinformation tweets, and the top-10 outlets account for over 95% of tweet volume.

estimates.measure_type: share of all disinformation-sharing tweets accounted for by the most active ~20% of the users who shared disinformation
estimates.value_raw: "approximately 20% of the community (~4k users) accounts for more than 90% of total tweets (~330k)"
estimates.conc_group_label: the most active ~20% of accounts sharing disinformation links (~4,000 of 23,243 users)
estimates.denominator: 354,746 tweets carrying links to 16,867 articles from 63 blacklisted Italian disinformation websites, posted by 23,243 unique users, 1 January - 27 May 2019
estimates.definition: a tweet counted if it contained an explicit URL to an article published on one of the blacklisted disinformation websites; users ranked by the number of such tweets they posted
estimates.misinfo_def: "we manually curated a list of websites which have been flagged by fact-checking agencies for fabricating and spreading a variety of malicious information, namely inaccurate and misleading news reports, hyper-partisan and propaganda stories, hoaxes and conspiracy theories. Differently from [8], satire was excluded from the analysis."
estimates.source_quote: In fact, approximately 20% of the community (∼4k users) accounts for more than 90% of total tweets (∼330k), in accordance with similar findings elsewhere [10, 9, 8].
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Source-based labelling with no article-level verification: a manually curated list of 63 Italian disinformation websites still active in January 2019, drawn from blacklists kept by Italian fact-checking organisations (butac.net, bufale.net, pagellapolitica.it); satire excluded. "we do not verify each news article manually but we assign the disinformation label to all items published on websites labeled as such". No reliability statistics; the authors concede the source-based assumption "might not be always true".
estimates.moderator_quote: As a matter of fact, using the standard streaming endpoint allows to gather 100% of shared tweets matching the defined query [27, 28, 8].
estimates.notes: Both quantities R1 requires are stated verbatim in one sentence (20% of users, >90% of tweets), so this row is clean. Note the denominator universe is users who shared AT LEAST ONE disinformation link, not the Italian Twitter population - so this is concentration WITHIN the sharing community, which is the strictest and least flattering framing (concentration measured against all Twitter users would be far more extreme). A looser restatement appears in the dismantling section: 'a few thousand nodes account for more than 75% of the total number of tweets shared in the five months before the elections', and in 'User activity': 'over 3/4 of the total number of tweets was shared by less than 4 thousand users (Medium, High and Extreme activity)' - compatible with, and weaker than, the entered figure.

estimates.definition: outlets ranked by the total number of tweets sharing their articles; the top 10 accounted for over 95% of that volume
estimates.misinfo_def: "we manually curated a list of websites which have been flagged by fact-checking agencies for fabricating and spreading a variety of malicious information, namely inaccurate and misleading news reports, hyper-partisan and propaganda stories, hoaxes and conspiracy theories."
estimates.source_quote: We show the time series for the daily engagement of Top-10 sources, which account for over 95% of total tweets, in Fig 4.

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator. The paper states the GROUP as a count ('Top-10 sources'), not as a percentage, which R1 normally treats as unusable. I converted it using the paper's own source universe (63 blacklisted websites compiled in January 2019, one more - ilprimatonazionale.it - added at the end of April), giving conc_group_pct = 10/63 = 15.9%. Two caveats: (a) it is not stated how many of the 63 sites actually had at least one shared article, so 15.9% is an UPPER bound on the group size, i.e. the concentration is at least this strong; (b) Fig 3's caption says Top-11 rather than Top-10 for the same >95% claim, and ilprimatonazionale.it was excluded from the engagement analysis despite ~30k associated tweets. If the project's rule is that a bare count of sources cannot be converted, drop this row and keep only the user-level one. A stricter alternative that needs no conversion beyond 1/63 = 1.6%: voxnews.info alone accounted for over 50% of all tweets.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NO PREVALENCE ESTIMATE EXISTS in this paper and none should be constructed. The corpus is built by querying the Twitter Streaming API for the blacklisted domains themselves, so it is an all-disinformation corpus with no denominator of Italian political or election-related tweets - exactly the 'all-false corpora with no denominator' case. The abstract's claims that disinformation 'had a limited impact on online discussions on the up-coming elections' and was 'confined in a limited community' are qualitative in this text; no share of the overall conversation is ever reported. (2) 'articles devoted to debunk false claims were barely engaged, accounting only for 6% of the total volume of tweets spreading disinformation in the same period' (23,215 fact-checking tweets vs 354,746 disinformation tweets) is the ratio of DEBUNKING to disinformation, not a misinformation share of anything - no row. (3) Further concentration statements that R8/R1 block: 'a minority of very active users (the ensemble with High and Extreme activity) accounts for half of the deceptive stories that were shared' - the group size would require summing two verbatim category counts (~500 High + 20 Extreme users), a cross-category sum; 'eliminating a few hundred nodes with largest values of Out-Degree... these users alone account for 90% of the total number of interactions between users' - 'a few hundred' is not a stated share and the activity measured is network interactions, not sharing; the k-core (218 nodes, k=47) and the website main core (35 nodes, k=14) are structural, not concentration shares. (4) The activity-class breakdown (Rare ~9.5k users with 1 tweet; Low ~8k; Medium ~3k; High ~500; Extreme exactly 20; 'About 1 user out of 5 shared more than 10 disinformation articles in five months'; 'The majority of the accounts (more than 75%) occasionally engaged with malicious content, sharing less than 10 stories each') describes the distribution of sharers within the disinformation community, not prevalence - potentially useful context for a concentration figure but not itself a top-X/Y-share statement. (5) Bot prevalence: only 2 of the 218 main-core accounts exceeded Botometer CAP 50% (58% and 64%), contrasted with ~25% in the US network of ref [8] - a bot share, not a misinformation share, so out of scope. (6) Account statuses (21,124 active, 800 deleted, 124 protected, 112 suspended; 20 verified; verified accounts involved in 5,761 tweets, 18 as author) are not misinformation shares. (7) Retweeting behaviour ('more than 60% of the accounts exhibit a re-tweeting activity larger than 0.95') is a behavioural distribution within the sharing community. (8) Recently created accounts 'account for 15% (around 18k tweets) of the total volume of tweets' - a share of disinformation tweets attributable to new accounts; this is an actor-composition share inside an all-false corpus, not a prevalence or a top-group concentration, so no row (an adjudicator could treat it as a concentration-adjacent figure, but the group is defined by account age, not by rank). (9) Topic composition (Fig 6, five topics) is reported only as a stacked-area chart - no readable numbers. (10) Trust-in-news figures (40% trust news, 23% trust news on social media; Twitter 8% vs Facebook 54% for news use) come from the Reuters Digital News Report - cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. (11) Facebook comparison is descriptive only (two outlets, Fig 2 time series), with no share. (12) All figures (1-12) are images and no value was taken from them except the Fig 3 caption text.

rob.design: Observational platform-data study, arXiv preprint (v2, 28 October 2019). Frame: Twitter Streaming API queried on the domains of 63 manually curated Italian disinformation websites active in January 2019 (list built from blacklists of Italian fact-checking organisations butac.net, bufale.net, pagellapolitica.it, covering hyper-partisan and conspiratorial news, hoaxes and pseudo-science, with satire explicitly excluded), plus 4 fact-checking domains for comparison; the standard streaming endpoint returns 100% of tweets matching the query, so the corpus is a census conditional on the domain list. Yield: 16,867 disinformation articles shared in 354,746 tweets by 23,243 unique users, 1 January - 27 May 2019 (figures label the window 07/01-27/05/2019); URL duplicates resolved by comparing HTML content; user profiles and timelines collected via the Twitter API (only for active, non-protected accounts). Labelling is purely source-based with no article-level verification and no inter-coder reliability; the authors acknowledge that mainstream outlets also carry misinformation and that the source assumption may fail. Analysis: diffusion network over ~20k nodes and ~100k edges, k-core decomposition, Louvain communities, In/Out-strength, betweenness and PageRank centralities, Mann-Kendall trend tests with Bonferroni correction, degree-preserving randomisation with Z-tests, Botometer CAP>50% (language-independent features) for bot detection. Key generalisability limit stated by the authors: Twitter carries only 8% of Italian online news users, far behind Facebook (54%) and WhatsApp (27%), and a Facebook comparison for two outlets suggests stronger reach there. No ethics approval needed (public data).
rob.item6_quote: To collect relevant data, we manually curated a list of websites which have been flagged by fact-checking agencies for fabricating and spreading a variety of malicious information, namely inaccurate and misleading news reports, hyper-partisan and propaganda stories, hoaxes and conspiracy theories.
rob.item10_quote: We collected 16,867 disinformation articles shared over 354,746 tweets by 23,243 unique users, and 1,743 fact-checking posts shared over 23,215 tweets by 9814 unique users.
